source.title: The Rate-Distortion-Polysemanticity Tradeoff in SAEs
source.authors: Tommaso Mencattini; Francesco Montagna; Francesco Locatello

record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes feature splitting and argues that polysemantic solutions depend on concept co-occurrence in the data, rather than being merely an optimization artifact. Its results are theoretical and synthetic; it does not test a dictionary-size sweep.
record.gate_note: The paper gives analytic conditions under which specified feature-splitting codes outperform monosemantic codes, and reports a synthetic RDP sweep. The Gemma SAEBench proxy audit does not measure feature splitting itself, so those proxy scores are not rows for these claim versions.
record.test_reason: Closed-form toy analysis (Section E.3) shows a feature-splitting code beats a monosemantic one under a TopK rate cap exactly when co-occurrence probabilities exceed stated bounds. The split atoms are not ground-truth concepts, so this bears on V6's mechanism. The study also argues the driver is joint occurrence, not correlation. There is no dictionary-size sweep and no trained LLM SAE splitting measurement.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Under toy assumptions, polysemanticity, including splitting and hedging, is the optimal response of a rate-constrained SAE to concept co-occurrence in the data, not an optimizer accident. Real-world proxy metrics mostly fail the RDP consistency check. The authors frame polysemanticity as a data problem and call for data-aware architectures and training.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a formal toy DGP, analytic loss comparisons, and a synthetic TopK sweep; it does not reproduce a dictionary-size scaling experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: The splitting comparisons vary TopK K (1 or 2) and depend on the stated co-occurrence-probability inequalities. The synthetic frontier varies rate k and monosemanticity penalty λ.

fits_no_version.finding: Synthetic TopK sweep (n=20, R6, 7 seeds): tightening rate raises the polysemanticity floor, and at P0=0 the R–D frontier is a staircase.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Enforcing monosemanticity in SAEs costs rate or distortion, with the cost set by concept co-occurrence.

fits_no_version.finding: Width-3 Top-2 SAE dictionary rotates from monosemantic initialization to a polysemantic (hedged) configuration during training (Figure 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Feature hedging emerges in narrow SAEs to reduce distortion.

fits_no_version.finding: The SAEBench Splitting score agrees only weakly with the RDP direction: TopK Gemma V=0.441, ρ=+0.21; ReLU Gemma V=0.411, ρ=−0.11.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Validity of SAE polysemanticity proxy metrics.

record.problems: The strongest splitting results rely on a stylized toy model: orthogonal concepts, zero biases, and aligned binary atoms. The synthetic experiment reports 7 seeds but no uncertainty estimates in the text. The real-world analysis uses precomputed SAEBench results and does not directly measure splitting or compare objectives.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant outcome rows were left out. The Gemma SAEBench proxy audit is not a direct measurement of the splitting behavior or objective comparisons named in the versions.

untested.parts: No dictionary-size sweep, replacement of a coarse feature, input coverage or direction similarity.
No splitting measurement in large models or open SAE releases. The SAEBench audit uses the Splitting score only as a proxy.
No nested families, geometry or hierarchy.
No parent/child firing or absorption measurement.
No cross-size decomposition or novel-latent analysis.
No comparison of alternative objectives such as Matryoshka SAEs. No hierarchical inputs. No real LLM SAEs trained.

missing.what: Claim that splitting (like hedging) emerges in narrow SAEs and is not wide-SAE-only. This bears on the scope of the dictionary-size framing.

Argument that reducing polysemanticity without a rate or distortion cost requires changing the data, not the architecture or optimizer. This is relevant to V6's claim that objectives like Matryoshka reduce splitting. It is theoretical (Theorem 3) and untested empirically.

record.verdict_notes: The study's 'feature splitting' is a narrow-SAE code (an atom for vi+vj plus a fallback for vi), not splitting as a dictionary grows. This fits V6's mechanism, not V1. The reader's 'challenges' label misreads 'not an optimization artifact': the authors mean the split arises as the objective's optimum, which supports V6's claim that it comes from the objective rather than model units. No numbers or uncertainty are given for the synthetic sweep.

versions.untested_parts: No comparison of increasing dictionary sizes, replacement of a smaller-dictionary feature, or measurement that split features cover the same inputs and lie near the smaller feature's direction.
No test of the splitting pattern at scale or across open SAE releases.
No test of nested feature families, geometric closeness, or correspondence to a hierarchy of model concepts.
No measurement of parent-child firing or tests of whether size or sparsity changes fix absorption.
No cross-dictionary decomposition of larger-SAE latents into smaller-SAE latents, or assessment of novel latents and dictionary completeness.
The study does not compare alternative objectives such as Matryoshka SAEs, test hierarchical inputs, or establish how the toy-model findings relate to units in real language models.

rows.subject: three-concept DGP
rows.operation_detail: Analytically compare the reconstruction loss of a feature-splitting code with a monosemantic code.
rows.measure: Difference in reconstruction loss: monosemantic minus feature-splitting code
rows.value: The difference is positive iff pi + pij > pj + pk + 2pjk.
rows.note: The result is conditional on the stated probability inequality and toy-model assumptions; it is an analytic comparison, not a measured training outcome.
rows.check: Analytic iff-condition, not a measurement. Splitting is optimal only when the inequality holds. The setting is narrow (m=2, n=3), not a growing dictionary.

rows.subject: synthetic DGP
rows.operation_detail: Sweep TopK rate and monosemanticity penalty to obtain an empirical RDP frontier.
rows.value: The text reports that tightening rate raises the monosemanticity floor, and that improving monosemanticity at fixed distortion costs rate; at P0=0 the R–D frontier is a staircase.
rows.note: The plotted sweep is described qualitatively; the study attributes the size of the premium to co-occurrence probabilities. The result is synthetic and does not compare objectives.
rows.check: The sweep measures a generic polysemanticity score P against rate and distortion. It does not measure feature splitting, so it should not link to V6. Moved to fits_no_version.

relationships.condition: Three-concept orthogonal toy DGP, m=2, TopK K∈{1,2}, Assumptions 1–4
relationships.reason: r1–r5: the rate-constrained MSE objective makes a splitting code (vi+vj plus a fallback) optimal when concepts co-occur enough. These atoms are not ground-truth concepts, so splitting comes from the objective interacting with the data.
relationships.display_finding: The rate-constrained MSE objective made a splitting code (vi+vj plus a fallback) optimal when concepts co-occurred often enough. These atoms are not ground-truth concepts, so the splitting comes from the objective interacting with the data.

relationships.reason: r1–r5 conditions use raw joint probabilities (pij, pijk), not correlation. Authors say correlation-based accounts are 'at best a proxy', so V6's 'correlated inputs' needs restating as co-occurrence. The text also argues splitting arises in narrow SAEs.
relationships.display_finding: The conditions for splitting are stated in raw joint probabilities (pij, pijk) rather than correlation, which the authors call 'at best a proxy', so 'correlated inputs' is better put as co-occurrence. The paper also argues that splitting arises in narrow SAEs.

relation.reason: Its own analytic results bear directly on whether the SAE objective produces splitting (V6).

tranche.reason: Closed-form analysis (Sec. 3.3, E.3) argues splitting follows from co-occurrence under a rate cap, with correlation 'at best a proxy', so V6's wording needs restating.

source_check.notes: All five inequalities match Section E.3 exactly. They are analytic results for n=3, m=2, with atoms restricted to unit-weight concept sums (Assumption 4), not measured training. Each one compares a splitting code only with the best monosemantic code. So 'optimal' strictly means 'beats the best monosemantic code': a hedged code could still be better. The main text points to an E.3 counterexample (hedging under zero correlation), but that counterexample concerns hedging, not splitting, and does not appear in the extracted E.3. The takeaway that only changing the data, not the architecture, reduces polysemanticity at fixed rate and distortion is in tension with V6's Matryoshka clause. The paper does not test that clause.
